pick-machine.title: Decide which machine to use
pick-machine.why: Every step after this one needs a machine that stays on and can take an SSH connection: a Mac you leave running, a Linux box you administer yourself, or a cloud VPS.
pick-machine.verifyHint: Answer the question above: whether the machine you have, or plan to get, is a Mac, a Linux box, or a VPS.
pick-machine.failHint: If you have none of the three, renting the cheapest cloud VPS is usually fastest. Once it answers SSH, follow the Linux box instructions in the next step.

enable-ssh-mac.title: Turn on Remote Login on the Mac
enable-ssh-mac.why: macOS ships with the SSH service switched off. This command does what System Settings → General → Sharing does when you enable Remote Login, which is what lets Agentmux reach the machine over SSH later.
enable-ssh-mac.verifyHint: Open Terminal on that same Mac and run the verification command. If it prints your username instead of an error, the SSH service is running.
enable-ssh-mac.failHint: If it says Connection refused, check that your account is on the allowed-users list under System Settings → General → Sharing.

enable-ssh-linux.title: Enable the SSH service on the Linux box
enable-ssh-linux.why: Most distributions don't ship the SSH service preinstalled, and the package name, the service name, and the command that starts services all differ. Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, RHEL, and Arch use systemd; Alpine uses OpenRC and has no systemctl at all. Each line below installs the service, enables it at boot, and starts it now, so run only the line for your distribution and skip the other three.
enable-ssh-linux.verifyHint: What a good result looks like depends on your distribution. On the systemd ones (Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, RHEL, Arch) you get a status block for ssh.service or sshd.service with the line Active: active (running); press q if the output opens in a pager. On Alpine you get one line like * status: started. Either one is enough.
enable-ssh-linux.failHint: If the service is installed and reported as running but you still can't connect, the cause is usually a firewall between you and the machine, or a cloud provider security group that hasn't opened the port. Check it one hop at a time to find where it stops. A minimal Alpine install has no sudo: if you see sudo: not found you are almost certainly root, so drop the leading sudo and run the line again.

vps-ssh-ready.title: Confirm the VPS already accepts SSH
vps-ssh-ready.why: Cloud VPS images almost always run the SSH service from the start, and the provider hands you a password or a key when the machine is created. Unlike a machine you set up yourself, there is nothing to install or switch on.
vps-ssh-ready.verifyHint: Connect with the credentials the provider gave you and run the verification command. A username in return means SSH works on this machine.
vps-ssh-ready.failHint: If you can't connect, check the firewall or security group rules in the provider's console and make sure the SSH port is open. That is where a VPS most often stops you, not the SSH configuration itself.

enable-ssh-windows.title: Turn on the SSH server in Windows
enable-ssh-windows.why: Windows 10 and 11 carry an OpenSSH Server as an optional feature, switched off by default. Run the three lines in one PowerShell window opened as administrator: the first installs it, the second starts it now, the third starts it again after every reboot. A Windows PC updates and reboots on a schedule of its own, so that third line is not optional.
enable-ssh-windows.verifyHint: Run the verification command in PowerShell. Status Running together with StartType Automatic is the result you want: SSH answers now, and it answers again after a reboot. The installer added an inbound firewall rule named OpenSSH-Server-In-TCP along the way.
enable-ssh-windows.failHint: Add-WindowsCapability needs administrator rights and a machine that can reach Windows Update. If it reports the capability as unknown, check that this is Windows 10 1809 or newer. If SSH answers on the PC but not from your phone, the firewall is the next suspect.

keep-awake-windows.title: Stop the PC from sleeping
keep-awake-windows.why: A multiplexer keeps an agent alive through a dropped connection, not through a sleeping machine. While the PC sleeps the agent is frozen and nothing on the phone can reach it, which is the whole reason you are setting this up. These two lines set sleep and hibernate to Never while the charger is in.
keep-awake-windows.verifyHint: Run the verification command. Current AC Power Setting Index: 0x00000000 means Never on AC power; any other value is a number of seconds.
keep-awake-windows.failHint: A machine on a work account can have sleep put back by a group policy, which overrides what you just set, so look again the next morning. Check Windows Update's active hours too: a reboot closes every session, and that is a different failure from a dropped connection.

install-agent.title: Install the agent you picked on the machine
install-agent.why: Agentmux attaches to a CLI agent that already runs on your machine; it doesn't install one or sign you in. Follow the official install instructions for the tool you picked, and get it installed and signed in on that machine first.
install-agent.verifyHint: Run the verification command. A printed path means at least one agent command is where this account's PATH can find it; nothing printed means the command is missing.
install-agent.failHint: If the command works in a terminal you opened yourself but not over SSH, the PATH is probably set only for interactive logins, not a broken install. The absolute path works either way.

install-agent-windows.title: Install the agent on the Windows machine
install-agent-windows.why: Agentmux attaches to a CLI agent that already runs on the machine; it does not install one or sign you in. Install the tool you picked with its own Windows instructions, into the account you will connect as. If Node.js is on the machine, most of them are one npm command.
install-agent-windows.verifyHint: Run the verification command in PowerShell or cmd. A printed path means the command is on this account's PATH; nothing printed means it is missing or outside PATH. Check the others the same way: where.exe codex, where.exe gemini, where.exe opencode.
install-agent-windows.failHint: If the command runs in a terminal you opened but Agentmux cannot find it, PATH is set for that shell only. Restart the SSH service so it reads the environment again: Restart-Service sshd. If that does not help, sign out and back in.

tmux-handled.title: tmux: nothing to do
tmux-handled.why: You don't need to install tmux yourself. Once Agentmux connects it installs tmux with whichever package manager the machine has (apt, dnf, yum, pacman, apk, brew, nix-env).
tmux-handled.verifyHint: Nothing to do in this step. Move on to the next one.
tmux-handled.failHint: If the app later reports that the automatic install failed, the cause is usually that sudo wants a TTY.

psmux-handled.title: psmux: nothing to do
psmux-handled.why: A Windows host has no tmux, so Agentmux uses psmux, a separate program with a command line modelled on tmux. It looks for psmux, pmux, or tmux.exe first, and installs one over winget, then Scoop, then cargo, whichever the machine already has.
psmux-handled.verifyHint: Nothing to do in this step. If you want to look for yourself, run where.exe psmux: a printed path means it is there.
psmux-handled.failHint: If the app says none of winget, Scoop, or cargo was found, install it yourself: run the command in this step, or take a binary and add its folder to PATH, then reconnect.

tailscale-host.title: Install Tailscale on the machine and sign in
tailscale-host.why: To reach this machine from anywhere without exposing SSH to the public internet, put it on your Tailscale network. Scanning bots knock on every address on earth all day. Once the machine is installed and signed in to the same account, it gains a second, private address that only you can reach.
tailscale-host.verifyHint: Run the verification command. Seeing this machine in the list with an active status means Tailscale is running and has joined your network.
tailscale-host.failHint: If the status waits, or the machine never appears in the list, check that both ends are signed in to the same account. A mismatched account is the usual cause.

tailscale-ios.title: Install Tailscale on the iPhone or iPad and sign in
tailscale-ios.why: The phone needs Tailscale too, signed in to the same account. Only then do both devices sit on one private network, which is what lets Agentmux reach the machine you just set up.
tailscale-ios.verifyHint: Open the Tailscale app: the machine should be in the list, marked online.
tailscale-ios.failHint: A phone signed in to a different account never sees the machine, and neither device appears in the other's list.

find-lan-address.title: Find the Mac's address on your local network
find-lan-address.why: If you want to connect over the same Wi-Fi and skip Tailscale, you need the Mac's local IP first. Without an address, SSH has nowhere to go.
find-lan-address.verifyHint: Run this command. You get something like 192.168.1.23, and that is the address you'll use next.
find-lan-address.failHint: If nothing prints, this Mac isn't reaching the network through en0. Read the address under System Settings → Wi-Fi → Details instead.

find-lan-address-linux.title: Find the Linux box's address on your local network
find-lan-address-linux.why: Same as on the Mac: connecting over the same Wi-Fi or local network needs the machine's IP before SSH knows where to go.
find-lan-address-linux.verifyHint: This prints an IP for every network interface on the machine. The first is usually the local address, typically one starting 192.168.
find-lan-address-linux.failHint: If several addresses print, pick the one on your phone's subnet, for example another 192.168.1.x.

find-lan-address-windows.title: Find the PC's address on your local network
find-lan-address-windows.why: Connecting over the same Wi-Fi without Tailscale needs the PC's own IP address, because SSH has to dial something. A Windows machine usually has more than one address: Wi-Fi, ethernet, and whatever virtual adapters are installed.
find-lan-address-windows.verifyHint: This prints a block per adapter with its IPv4 address. Pick the one on the same network as your phone, for example another 192.168.1.x.
find-lan-address-windows.failHint: If nothing prints, that adapter is not connected. Run ipconfig by itself to see every adapter, or go through Tailscale, which does not care which adapter carries the traffic.

add-server.title: Add the server in Agentmux
add-server.why: Everything so far made the machine reachable. This step adds it in Agentmux: the host address, the account, and the connection method you just confirmed.
add-server.verifyHint: Agentmux connects as soon as you finish adding it. A connected status, plus a terminal you can see, means the whole setup worked.
add-server.failHint: If it can't connect, re-check each answer you gave in turn: SSH on the machine, the agent install, Tailscale. Usually a step above was missed.
